# SystemVerilog basics {#sec-sv-intro .unnumbered}

## Goal for this week

- Explain what a hardware description language is, and why we describe
  digital systems in text instead of drawing every gate
- Place SystemVerilog in the Verilog family, and know which subset of it
  this course uses
- Read and write a module: ports, directions, internal signals
- Tell nets from variables, and know the four values a signal can hold
- Write numeric constants with an explicit size and base
- Describe combinational logic with `assign` and the SystemVerilog
  operators, and avoid the classic mistakes: `&` vs. `&&`, and two drivers
  on one net

## Why describe hardware in text

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- A modern SoC has millions of gates: drawing them one by one does not scale
- A **hardware description language (HDL)** describes the structure and
  behavior of a digital system as text
- Tools turn the text into hardware (**synthesis**) or into a running model
  (**simulation**)
- *Abstraction*: say how the system works without getting consumed early
  by implementation details
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The previous chapters described digital circuits bottom-up: transistors,
gates, and the standard and programmable devices built from them, up to the
FPGA. Nobody designs a processor by placing those pieces one at a time. A modern SoC has millions
of gates, and a schematic of that size is neither writable nor reviewable.
Instead we describe the system in text, in a **hardware description
language** (HDL), and let tools do the placing.

The key idea is *abstraction*: an HDL lets us specify how a system
operates without getting consumed prematurely by how it is implemented.
The same description can be used in two very different ways. A **simulator**
runs it as a model, so we can check behavior long before any chip exists. A
**synthesizer** turns it into a netlist of real gates, or into the LUTs and
flip-flops of the FPGA from the previous chapter. The rest of this course
is about writing descriptions that are good for both.
:::

## What an HDL is used for

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
HDLs were designed to model behavior at several levels of abstraction:

- High-level behavioral modeling
- **RTL (register-transfer level)** modeling: what this course writes
- Gate- and transistor-level netlists
- Timing models for timing simulation
- Design verification (testbenches)
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A single HDL covers a wide range of jobs. At the top, we can write a
high-level behavioral model that says *what* a block computes, with no
hardware structure at all. One level down is **register-transfer level**
(RTL): the design is a set of registers, and the combinational logic that
moves data between them on each clock edge. This is the level at which this
course, and almost all digital design, is done. Below it, the output of
synthesis is a gate-level netlist, which can itself be written in the same
language, and which can be annotated with timing information for timing
simulation. Finally, the same language is used to write testbenches that
verify the design.

Not everything an HDL can express can be turned into hardware. A
simulator will happily run a testbench that waits 10 ns and prints a
message, but a synthesizer has no gate for "wait 10 ns". Only a *subset* of
the language is synthesizable, and writing in that subset is the first
skill of this course.
:::

## From Verilog to SystemVerilog

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **Verilog**: introduced in 1984, for two purposes
    - model digital systems
    - write testbenches to check them
- Synthesis supports only a subset of the language
- **SystemVerilog** (IEEE 1800) extends Verilog-2005
    - adds new hardware-modeling features
    - adds verification features (assertions, classes, randomization)
- Each standard extends the previous one: backward compatible
- This course: a **synthesizable subset** of SystemVerilog
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Verilog was introduced in 1984 with a dual purpose: to model digital
systems, and to describe the testbenches that check those models. As we saw,
synthesis supports only a subset of what the language can express.
Verilog was standardized several times, and the last Verilog standard is
the one that SystemVerilog builds on:

| Standard | Year | Nickname |
|---|---|---|
| IEEE 1364-1995 | 1995 | Verilog-1995 |
| IEEE 1364-2001 | 2001 | Verilog-2001 |
| IEEE 1364.1-2002 | 2002 | Verilog RTL Synthesis (patch for the synthesizable subset) |
| IEEE 1364-2005 | 2005 | Verilog-2005, the last Verilog standard |
| IEEE 1800-2005 | 2005 | SystemVerilog-2005, extensions of Verilog-2005 |
| IEEE 1800-2009, -2012, -2017, -2023 | | SystemVerilog, each extending the previous one |

Too many new features had accumulated to keep calling the result Verilog,
so a new language was defined. SystemVerilog extends Verilog in two
directions: it improves hardware modeling (for example `logic`,
`always_comb`, `always_ff`, enumerations and packed structures, all of
which we use), and it adds verification features such as assertions,
object-oriented programming, and constrained random stimulus.

Each SystemVerilog standard is an extension of the previous one, so
backward compatibility is preserved. A synthesizer for SystemVerilog-2005
understands plain Verilog, but a tool that only supports Verilog-2001 will
report an error on the first SystemVerilog construct it meets.

We will cover only a small, synthesizable part of the language. There are
two reasons. The language is far too large for one course. And once you can
prototype with the basic constructs, new ones are easy to pick up when you
need them.
:::

## Anatomy of a module

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module and_or (
    input  logic a, b, c,
    output logic y
);
  logic t;
  assign t = a & b;
  assign y = t | c;
endmodule
```

- `module` … `endmodule` encloses the description
- Ports: **direction**, **type**, name
- Modules can instantiate other modules: hierarchy
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Every piece of hardware in SystemVerilog lives inside a **module**. The
keywords `module` and `endmodule` mark the beginning and the end of the
description, and a module can instantiate other modules inside it, which
is how hierarchical designs are built.

```systemverilog
module and_or (
    input  logic a, b, c,
    output logic y
);
  logic t;                 // internal signal
  assign t = a & b;
  assign y = t | c;
endmodule
```

The module name is followed by a **port list** in parentheses. Each port
has a *direction*, a *type*, and a name. Several ports of the same
direction and type can share one declaration, as `a, b, c` do above. After
the semicolon comes the module body: declarations of internal signals such
as `t`, and the statements that describe behavior, here two continuous
assignments. @fig-and-or shows what a synthesis tool builds from this
module.

| Direction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `input` | Data flows into the module through this port |
| `output` | Data flows out of the module through this port |
| `inout` | Bidirectional: data can flow both ways (used for tri-state pins) |

![The `and_or` module, drawn by Yosys directly from the source above.](../images/rtl/and_or.svg){#fig-and-or width=60%}
:::

## Values: 0, 1, X and Z

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
A signal in SystemVerilog can hold one of **four values**:

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | logic low |
| `1` | logic high |
| `X` | unknown, or conflicting drivers |
| `Z` | high impedance: nothing drives the signal |

- Real hardware only has 0 and 1; `X` and `Z` exist to model what *could*
  go wrong
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A wire in a real circuit is at a high or a low voltage, so you might
expect two values, 0 and 1. SystemVerilog uses **four**, because the
simulator also has to represent situations that a real circuit can get
into:

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | logic low, false |
| `1` | logic high, true |
| `X` | unknown: an uninitialized register, or a net that two sources drive to different values |
| `Z` | high impedance: nothing is driving the signal (an unconnected input, or a tri-state buffer that is turned off) |

You will meet `X` in simulation when something is wrong, and it is one of
the most useful debugging signals you have: it spreads through logic that
depends on it, so an `X` on an output points back to an uninitialized or
double-driven source. `Z` appears with tri-state buffers, like the I/O
block of the FPGA chapter. A synthesizer never creates an `X` or a
`Z`; they exist only in the simulation model.
:::

## Data types: nets and variables

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- **Net** (`wire`): a physical connection
    - holds no value of its own
    - takes the resolved value of whatever drives it
    - driven by `assign` or by a module output
- **Variable** (`logic`, `int`, …): remembers the last value assigned to it
    - assigned in procedural blocks (`always_*`)
- `logic`: a 4-state type usable in both roles, with **one driver only**
- `bit`: a 2-state type (0 and 1 only)
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
SystemVerilog has two kinds of signals, and the difference between them is
what the whole language is built around.

A **net**, declared with `wire`, models a physical connection between
things. It stores nothing: its value at any moment is whatever its drivers
are producing right now. If several things drive it, the net resolves
their values, which is how a tri-state bus works. A **variable** is a
signal that *remembers*. It holds the last value assigned to it, and keeps
it until the next assignment.

| | Net (`wire`) | Variable (`logic`, `int`, …) |
|---|---|---|
| Models | a connection | a stored value |
| Holds a value | no, resolved from its drivers | yes, the last one assigned |
| Driven by | `assign`, module outputs | `assign` (once), or procedural blocks |
| Multiple drivers | allowed, resolved | an error |

In plain Verilog you had to choose between `wire` and `reg` depending on
*how you assigned* the signal, and `reg` was widely mistaken for "a
register" when it is nothing of the kind. SystemVerilog fixes this with
**`logic`**: a four-state data type that can be driven by a continuous
assignment, by a procedural block, or by a module output. Its one rule is
that it may have only one driver, and the tools check it. For a signal that
legitimately has several drivers, such as a tri-state bus, use `wire`.

`bit` is the two-state
counterpart of `logic`: it can only hold 0 and 1, so it can hide an
unknown value in simulation by silently turning it into a 0. For that
reason this course uses `logic` for signals.
:::

## Vectors and integer types

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
logic [7:0] data;     // 8-bit vector, bit 7 is the MSB
logic       valid;    // 1-bit signal

data[3]      // one bit
data[7:4]    // a part-select, 4 bits
```

| Type | Bits | Signed | States |
|---|---|---|---|
| `logic [n-1:0]` | n | no | 4 |
| `bit [n-1:0]` | n | no | 2 |
| `byte` / `shortint` | 8 / 16 | yes | 2 |
| `int` / `longint` | 32 / 64 | yes | 2 |
| `integer` | 32 | yes | 4 |
| `real` | 64 | n/a | simulation only |
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A signal declared with a range in square brackets is a **vector**:
`logic [7:0] data` is an 8-bit signal whose most significant bit is
`data[7]`. You can select a single bit, `data[3]`, or a contiguous slice,
`data[7:4]`. Vectors are unsigned unless declared otherwise.

The types we use most are summarized below. The integer types come from C,
and are mainly useful for loop counters and constants. Signals that
become wires and registers in hardware should be `logic` vectors, which
make the width explicit.

| Type | Bits | Signed | States |
|---|---|---|---|
| `logic [n-1:0]` | n | no | 4 (0, 1, X, Z) |
| `bit [n-1:0]` | n | no | 2 (0, 1) |
| `byte` | 8 | yes | 2 |
| `shortint` | 16 | yes | 2 |
| `int` | 32 | yes | 2 |
| `longint` | 64 | yes | 2 |
| `integer` | 32 | yes | 4 (legacy from Verilog) |
| `real` | 64, floating point | n/a | simulation only: not synthesizable |
:::

## Writing constants

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
`<size>'<base><value>`

```systemverilog
4'b1010        // binary
6'o12          // octal
8'd10          // decimal
8'hA           // hexadecimal
```

- All four above are the number **ten**
- Underscores are ignored: `8'b1010_1010`
- `10` alone is a **32-bit signed** decimal: always give a size
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A SystemVerilog constant carries its own width, written as
`<size>'<base><value>`, where `<size>` is the number of bits and `<base>` is
`b`, `o`, `d` or `h` for binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal. The four
constants below all have the value ten, but different widths:

```systemverilog
logic [3:0] binary_num  = 4'b1010;  // 4-bit binary 1010
logic [5:0] octal_num   = 6'o12;    // 6-bit octal 12
logic [7:0] decimal_num = 8'd10;    // 8-bit decimal 10
logic [7:0] hex_num     = 8'hA;     // 8-bit hexadecimal A
```

Underscores are ignored and are there for readability, so `8'b1010_1010`
is easier to read than `8'b10101010`. The characters `x` and `z` are
allowed in a constant: `4'b10xz`.

Always write the size. A bare number such as `10` is a **32-bit signed
decimal**, and silently mixing it with narrower signals is a common source
of width mismatches. If the value is bigger than the stated size, the extra
upper bits are discarded: `4'd20` is `4'b0100`. To fill every bit of a
signal of any width with the same value, use the unsized forms `'0` and `'1`.
:::

## Continuous assignment

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
assign out = a & b;
```

- The right side is **continuously** evaluated
- The left side is a **net** (or a `logic` with one driver)
- Models **combinational logic**
- It is not a statement that runs once
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The `assign` keyword connects a value to a signal **continuously**:

```systemverilog
assign out = a & b;   // out always equals a AND b
```

Whenever `a` or `b` changes, `out` changes with it. A continuous
assignment is not a step in a program. It is a gate that exists as long as
the circuit is powered, and it models combinational logic.
:::

## Not like assignment in C

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
assign b = a;
assign c = b;
```

- C: copy `a` into `b`, then `b` into `c`
- Hardware: two wires. Synthesis removes `b`: **`c = a`**
- The order of the lines does not matter
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A programming language would read the next two lines top to bottom:

```systemverilog
assign b = a;
assign c = b;
```

First copy `a` into `b`, then copy `b` into `c`. In hardware both lines
exist at the same time as two connections, and `b` is just the wire between
them. A synthesis tool removes it and infers `assign c = a`. For the same
reason, swapping the two lines changes nothing.
:::

## Two drivers on one net

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
wire c;
assign c = a;
assign c = b;
```

- C: the last assignment wins
- Hardware: **two outputs connected to one wire**
- If `a != b` the net is **`X`**
- With `logic`, the tool rejects the code outright
- Avoid at all costs
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The second example is the one that breaks C intuition completely:

```systemverilog
wire c;
assign c = a;
assign c = b;
```

In a programming language the second line would overwrite the first, and
`c` would end up with the value of `b`. In hardware, both lines are always
active, so the net `c` is **driven by two sources at once**. When `a` and
`b` agree, nothing is wrong. When they differ, one source pulls the wire
high while the other pulls it low, and the simulator reports an unknown
value `X` (@fig-two-drivers). In a real circuit, this is a short circuit
between two gate outputs.

![A net driven by `a` and by `b`: whenever they disagree, `c` is `X`.](../images/waves/two_drivers.svg){#fig-two-drivers}

If `c` were declared as `logic`, the tool would reject the second
assignment at compile time, because a `logic` signal may have only one
driver. That is the reason to prefer `logic`: it turns a silent `X` in
simulation into an error you see immediately. This situation must be
avoided in every design that is not a deliberate tri-state bus.
:::

## Operators at a glance

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
| Family | Operators | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Arithmetic | `+ - * / %` | number |
| Bitwise | `& \| ^ ~` | same width as operands |
| Reduction | `& \| ^ ~& ~\| ~^` | **1 bit** |
| Logical | `&& \|\| !` | **1 bit** |
| Relational | `== != < <= > >=` | 1 bit |
| Shift | `<< >> <<< >>>` | width of left operand |
| Conditional | `? :` | width of the branches |
| Concatenation | `{a, b}` `{n{a}}` | sum of the parts |
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
SystemVerilog has a rich set of operators, most of them familiar from C.
The best way to keep them straight is to group them by *what they
return*, because the most common mistakes come from expecting one width
and getting another.

| Family | Operators | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Arithmetic | `+ - * / %` | a number, sized by the surrounding expression |
| Bitwise | `& \| ^ ~` | same width as the operands, computed bit by bit |
| Reduction | `& \| ^ ~& ~\| ~^` | 1 bit |
| Logical | `&& \|\| !` | 1 bit (true or false) |
| Relational | `== != < <= > >=` | 1 bit |
| Shift | `<< >> <<< >>>` | width of the left operand |
| Conditional | `? :` | width of the chosen branch |
| Concatenation, replication | `{a, b}`, `{n{a}}` | sum of the parts |

The sections below take them in turn. Hardware cost matters here: each
operator becomes real logic, so `a + b` is an adder and `a * b` is a
multiplier, and a division by a non-constant is expensive enough that you
should hesitate before writing it.
:::

## Bitwise vs. logical

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
logic [3:0] a = 4'b1010;
logic [3:0] b = 4'b0101;

a & b     // 4'b0000   bit by bit
a && b    // 1'b1      both are non-zero: true AND true
```

- `&` `|` `^` `~`: work **bit by bit**, result as wide as the operands
- `&&` `||` `!`: treat each operand as **true or false**, result is 1 bit
- Mixing them up is the most common beginner error
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The bitwise operators `&`, `|`, `^` and `~` work on each bit position
separately, and the result is as wide as the operands. The logical
operators `&&`, `||` and `!` treat each whole operand as a single truth
value (zero is false, anything else is true) and return one bit.

```systemverilog
logic [3:0] a = 4'b1010;
logic [3:0] b = 4'b0101;

assign x = a & b;     // 4'b0000: no bit position has a 1 in both
assign y = a && b;    // 1'b1: a is non-zero, and so is b
```

Both lines look like "a AND b", and they give opposite answers. For
single-bit signals the two are interchangeable, which is why mixing them up
usually goes unnoticed until the signals become vectors. Use `&` and `|`
for data, and `&&` and `||` only in conditions.
:::

## Reduction, relational and shift operators

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
logic [5:0] a = 6'b101010;

&a      // 1'b0   AND of all bits
|a      // 1'b1   OR of all bits
^a      // 1'b1   XOR of all bits: parity

a == b      // equality, 1 bit
a >= b      // comparison, 1 bit
a << 2      // shift left by 2
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A **reduction** operator is a bitwise operator written with a single
operand. It combines all the bits of a vector into one:

```systemverilog
logic [5:0] a = 6'b101010;
logic c, d, e;

assign c = &a;   // AND of all bits: 0
assign d = |a;   // OR of all bits: 1
assign e = ^a;   // XOR of all bits: 1, the parity of a
```

Reduction operators are a compact way to write a wide gate: `&a` is a
six-input AND, and `^a` is a parity tree.

The **relational** operators `== != < <= > >=` compare two values and
return one bit. `==` gives `X` if either operand has an `X` or `Z` bit.
There is also a case-equality operator, `===`, that compares `X` and `Z`
literally, but it exists only for simulation and is not synthesizable. The
**shift** operators move the bits of a vector: `<<` and `>>` shift in
zeros, and `<<<` and `>>>` are the arithmetic versions, which keep the
sign bit of a signed operand when shifting right.

Operator precedence mostly follows C, but you should not rely on
remembering it. Add parentheses.
:::

## Conditional operator, concatenation and replication

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
assign c = (a > b) ? 1'b1 : 1'b0;      // select

assign w = {a, b};      // concatenate: 4'b1010, 4'b0101 -> 8'b10100101
assign e = {3{d}};      // replicate:   2'b11 -> 6'b111111
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The **conditional** operator `cond ? x : y` selects between two values. In
hardware it is a multiplexer: both `x` and `y` exist, and `cond` chooses
which one reaches the output. It can be nested, which is how we build
larger multiplexers below.

The **concatenation** operator `{}` joins bits, vectors or expressions into
one longer vector. The **replication** operator `{n{...}}` repeats a value
`n` times:

```systemverilog
logic [3:0] a = 4'b1010;
logic [3:0] b = 4'b0101;
logic [7:0] c;
logic [1:0] d = 2'b11;
logic [5:0] e;

assign c = {a, b};     // 8'b10100101
assign e = {3{d}};     // 6'b111111
```

Concatenation is also valid on the left of an assignment, which we use
below to capture the carry of an adder.
:::

## Example: 4-bit 4:1 multiplexer

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module mux4to1 (
    input  logic [3:0] in0, in1, in2, in3,
    input  logic [1:0] sel,
    output logic [3:0] out
);
  assign out = (sel == 2'b00) ? in0 :
               (sel == 2'b01) ? in1 :
               (sel == 2'b10) ? in2 :
                                in3;
endmodule
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A 4-bit, 4-input multiplexer passes one of four 4-bit inputs to the output,
chosen by a 2-bit select signal. Built from nested conditional operators:

```systemverilog
module mux4to1 (
    input  logic [3:0] in0, in1, in2, in3,   // four 4-bit data inputs
    input  logic [1:0] sel,                  // 2-bit select
    output logic [3:0] out                   // 4-bit output
);
  assign out = (sel == 2'b00) ? in0 :
               (sel == 2'b01) ? in1 :
               (sel == 2'b10) ? in2 :
                                in3;
endmodule
```

Each `?:` tests one value of `sel` and, if it does not match, hands the
decision to the next. The last branch, `in3`, is the default that is taken
when no earlier condition is true, so there is always a value for `out`.
The synthesized result is in @fig-mux4to1. Compare it with the 2-to-1
multiplexer written with `always_comb` in the next chapter: same hardware,
different notation.

![The `mux4to1` module as drawn by Yosys.](../images/rtl/mux4to1.svg){#fig-mux4to1}
:::

## Example: 4-bit adder

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module adder4bit (
    input  logic [3:0] a, b,
    output logic [3:0] sum,
    output logic       carry_out
);
  logic c1, c2, c3;

  assign sum[0] = a[0] ^ b[0];
  assign c1     = a[0] & b[0];

  assign sum[1] = a[1] ^ b[1] ^ c1;
  assign c2     = (a[1] & b[1]) | (c1 & (a[1] ^ b[1]));
  // ... bits 2 and 3 follow the same pattern
endmodule
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The adder adds two 4-bit numbers and produces a 4-bit sum and a carry-out
bit. We build it exactly as on paper: a half adder for the least
significant bit, then a full adder for each following bit, with an
internal carry wire `c1`, `c2`, `c3` passed from one stage to the next.

```systemverilog
module adder4bit (
    input  logic [3:0] a, b,
    output logic [3:0] sum,
    output logic       carry_out
);
  logic c1, c2, c3;                       // carries between stages

  // Half adder: least significant bit
  assign sum[0] = a[0] ^ b[0];
  assign c1     = a[0] & b[0];

  // Full adders
  assign sum[1] = a[1] ^ b[1] ^ c1;
  assign c2     = (a[1] & b[1]) | (c1 & (a[1] ^ b[1]));

  assign sum[2] = a[2] ^ b[2] ^ c2;
  assign c3     = (a[2] & b[2]) | (c2 & (a[2] ^ b[2]));

  assign sum[3]    = a[3] ^ b[3] ^ c3;
  assign carry_out = (a[3] & b[3]) | (c3 & (a[3] ^ b[3]));
endmodule
```

Writing out the gate equations is useful once, to see what an adder is.
In practice we let the tool do it. The `+` operator, with a concatenation on
the left to catch the carry, describes the same adder in one line:

```systemverilog
assign {carry_out, sum} = a + b;
```

The 5-bit result of `a + b` is split across the 1-bit `carry_out` and the
4-bit `sum`. @fig-adder-gates shows the hand-built carry chain, and
@fig-adder-plus the single adder block that a synthesis tool is free to map
onto the dedicated carry logic of an FPGA.

![The gate-level `adder4bit`: a half adder followed by three full adders, with the carry rippling from bit to bit.](../images/rtl/adder4bit.svg){#fig-adder-gates}

![The same adder written with the `+` operator.](../images/rtl/adder4bit_plus.svg){#fig-adder-plus width=60%}
:::

## From modules to behavior

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- Everything so far was **combinational**, written with `assign`
- Next chapter: bigger combinational blocks with `always_comb`, and
  state with `always_ff`
- Rule of thumb: **`assign` / `always_comb` for logic, `always_ff` for
  registers**
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Everything we wrote in this chapter is combinational: outputs depend only
on the current inputs, and nothing remembers anything. That was enough to
describe multiplexers and adders, but a processor also needs state. The next
chapter introduces the procedural blocks that describe it: `always_comb`
for larger combinational descriptions, and `always_ff` for registers that
update on a clock edge. The one rule to carry forward is that each hardware
element has exactly one notation, `assign` or `always_comb` for logic and
`always_ff` for registers.
:::
